items.explanation: The textbook's claim fails on the evidence: the Compromise bought only a few years of quiet at a terrible price. Its Fugitive Slave Act made Northerners legal participants in catching runaways, and outrage at that requirement converted many previously indifferent Northerners into abolitionists — the opposite of settling the question.
items.fact_source: u5.md §The story — the Compromise of 1850 bought a few years of quiet at a terrible price: Northerners were now legally required to help catch runaways, and many who had never cared about abolition became abolitionists out of outrage; §Key terms (Fugitive Slave Act)

option_explanations.A: Wrong because sectional debate intensified within four years, producing Bleeding Kansas and a sectional party.
option_explanations.B: Right because the Fugitive Slave Act's enforcement requirement radicalized Northern opinion instead of calming it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because abolitionists were not satisfied; the Act's brutality angered them further.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Compromise of 1850 was passed as a package of measures.

options: (A) The claim is accurate: the Compromise ended all sectional debate until the Civil War began in 1861
(B) The claim is inaccurate: the Fugitive Slave Act's rendition requirement radicalized Northern opinion
(C) The claim is accurate: California's admission as a free state fully satisfied the abolitionist movement
(D) The claim is inaccurate: the Compromise was never actually passed by Congress in any form
items.stem: A textbook claims the Compromise of 1850 'settled the slavery question for a generation.' Which of the following best evaluates that claim in context?

stimulus.text: The Compromise of 1850: California admitted free, the rest of the Mexican Cession left to popular sovereignty — and a strict new Fugitive Slave Act requiring Northerners to assist in capturing escaped enslaved people.

items.explanation: The Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed the Missouri Compromise's 36°30′ geographic line and substituted popular sovereignty — letting settlers vote slavery up or down. That turned every territorial organization into a direct contest over slavery's future, which is why armed partisans flooded Kansas.
items.fact_source: u5.md §The story — the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed the Missouri Compromise's 36°30′ line outright, letting settlers vote slavery up or down; settlers on both sides flooded Kansas and started killing each other; §Key terms (Kansas-Nebraska Act, Bleeding Kansas)

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the Supreme Court issued no such order regarding Kansas settlement.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because Mexico never invaded Kansas Territory.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Act repealed the 36°30′ line; that repeal is what created the crisis.
option_explanations.D: Right because replacing a geographic settlement with popular sovereignty made each territory a battleground over slavery.

options: (A) The Supreme Court had ordered all settlers to leave Kansas Territory immediately
(B) Mexico invaded Kansas Territory to reclaim it
(C) The Missouri Compromise's 36°30′ line was still in force, and both sides took up arms to defend it
(D) Repealing the 36°30′ line for popular sovereignty made each territory a slavery battleground
items.stem: After the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, proslavery and antislavery settlers flooded Kansas Territory and began killing each other in 'Bleeding Kansas.' Which broader development best explains this violence?

stimulus.text: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) organized the territories on popular sovereignty, repealing the Missouri Compromise line; rival settlers poured into Kansas and 'Bleeding Kansas' followed.

items.explanation: Reagan's firing of the illegally striking controllers was a deliberate signal: organized labor's postwar power was over. It belongs to the New Right's broader redefinition of government's role — cutting taxes, slashing regulation, and shrinking domestic government after the New Deal era.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — breaking the PATCO air-traffic controllers' strike to signal that organized labor's power was over; §Key terms (PATCO strike, 1981 — a landmark defeat for organized labor)

option_explanations.A: Right because the firing was a symbolic break with the New Deal labor order, central to Reagan's conservative program.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because strikes long predated 1981 in American history.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the Soviet Union collapsed a decade later, for unrelated reasons.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the firing was a labor action, not the deregulation of the airline industry itself.

options: (A) It signaled the New Right's attack on big government and labor's postwar power
(B) It was the first labor strike in American history
(C) It caused the immediate collapse of the Soviet Union and the sudden end of the Cold War
(D) It ended all federal regulation of the airline industry permanently
items.stem: In 1981, President Reagan fired striking air-traffic controllers (PATCO) who had walked out illegally. Which broader development best explains the historical significance of this action?

stimulus.image_caption: President Reagan addresses the press in the Rose Garden regarding the 1981 air-traffic controllers' strike.

items.explanation: Reagan's challenge came during the Cold War endgame: Gorbachev's reforms were shaking the USSR from within while sustained American pressure — the military buildup, SDI, and arms negotiations like the INF Treaty of 1987 — pressed from without. The exam rewards this multi-causal account over single-hero stories.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — Reagan called the Soviet Union an 'evil empire,' announced SDI (1983), then negotiated seriously with Gorbachev, signing the INF Treaty in 1987; §What the exam tests here — explain why the Cold War ended: internal Soviet decay and Gorbachev's reforms alongside American pressure

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the United States never recognized East Germany as legitimate in this way.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because Reagan did not withdraw from NATO; he maintained the alliance.
option_explanations.C: Right because the speech belongs to the endgame shaped by both Soviet reform and American pressure.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Wall fell in November 1989, two years after the speech.

options: (A) The United States had just formally recognized East Germany as a legitimate sovereign state
(B) Reagan was announcing an American withdrawal from the NATO alliance
(C) The Cold War endgame of Gorbachev's reforms plus American pressure and arms negotiations
(D) The Berlin Wall had already fallen by the time Reagan spoke
items.stem: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' — Ronald Reagan, West Berlin, June 1987. Which broader development best explains the context of this statement?

stimulus.image_caption: President Reagan at the Berlin Wall in June 1987, where he delivered the 'tear down this wall' address.

items.explanation: Berlin was divided because Germany was divided: after World War II the Allies split Germany, and the Cold War confrontation between the superpowers made the divided city the symbolic front line of a divided Europe, with the Wall (1961-1989) as its starkest marker.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989; Germany reunified; the Cold War's endgame

option_explanations.A: Wrong because Germany's division came from World War II and the Cold War, not World War I or France alone.
option_explanations.B: Right because the Wall embodied the superpower confrontation that split Germany and Europe.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because no such steel-tariff dispute explains the Wall.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because Germany was divided by the Allied powers in 1945, not by the United Nations in 1991.

options: (A) Germany's division was a punishment imposed solely by France after World War I ended
(B) The Cold War confrontation that divided Germany and made Berlin its symbolic front line
(C) A trade dispute between the United States and the Soviet Union over steel tariffs and exports
(D) The United Nations' decision to partition Germany into eastern and western zones in 1991
items.stem: This photograph shows East German guards at the Berlin Wall near Checkpoint Charlie. Which broader development best explains the context of this divided city?

stimulus.image_caption: East German guards at their post on the Berlin Wall near Checkpoint Charlie, Berlin.

items.explanation: NAFTA embodied the post-Cold War faith in globalization: with the Soviet Union gone and America the unchallenged superpower, the 1990s brought trade deals and institutions — NAFTA (1994), the WTO — integrating markets across borders, along with the discontents that later followed.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — NAFTA (1994) and the WTO embodied a new faith in globalization; §Key terms (NAFTA, Globalization)

option_explanations.A: Wrong because NAFTA lowered trade barriers; it was the opposite of 1930s protectionism.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the Cold War was over; NAFTA was an economic agreement, not a military alliance.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the agreement integrated the U.S. with world markets rather than isolating it.
option_explanations.D: Right because NAFTA was the signature trade pact of the 1990s globalization era.

options: (A) The return of 1930s-style protectionism and high tariffs
(B) A military alliance directed against the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact nations
(C) An effort to isolate the United States from world markets and trade
(D) The 1990s faith in globalization: market integration through NAFTA and the WTO

items.explanation: The historian's argument holds: the review explicitly frames Patriot Act surveillance as echoing earlier wartime expansions — the Espionage Act, internment, and McCarthyism. The recurring pattern is the tension between liberty and security, with crises repeatedly producing federal power at liberty's expense.
items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — compare 9/11's aftermath with earlier wartime expansions of federal power: Patriot Act surveillance and the security state echo the Espionage Act, internment, and McCarthyism

option_explanations.A: Right because earlier wars produced the same liberty-versus-security pattern the historian identifies.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because earlier wars did expand federal power, repeatedly.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because terrorism legislation predated 2001; the Patriot Act expanded existing powers.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Patriot Act expanded surveillance and detention powers.

options: (A) The argument holds: the Espionage Act, internment, and McCarthyism show the same wartime pattern
(B) The argument fails: no earlier American war ever expanded federal power in any way
(C) The argument is well supported: the Patriot Act was the first American law ever to address terrorism
(D) The argument fails: the Patriot Act reduced federal surveillance and detention powers
items.stem: After September 11, 2001, Congress passed the Patriot Act, expanding federal surveillance and detention powers. A historian argues this fits a recurring American pattern. Which of the following best evaluates that argument?

stimulus.image_caption: Ground Zero in New York City on September 14, 2001, three days after the attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people.

items.explanation: Reaganomics was the economic arm of the New Right's repudiation of New Deal and Great Society liberalism: where the earlier era answered 'what government is for' with active federal management, Reagan's program answered with tax cuts, deregulation, and domestic spending cuts. Growth returned, but so did huge deficits and inequality.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'Reaganomics' rested on supply-side theory: lower taxes would unleash growth that paid for itself; growth did return, but so did huge deficits and stark inequality; §What the exam tests here — compare Reagan's conservatism with the liberalism it displaced

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the Depression produced the interventionist liberalism Reaganomics repudiated.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the program came from the New Right, not from Democratic welfare expansion.
option_explanations.C: Right because supply-side economics reversed the New Deal/Great Society answer to what government is for.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the Federal Reserve never nationalized major banks.

options: (A) The Great Depression's demand for massive federal intervention in the economy
(B) The Democratic Party's embrace of larger welfare programs
(C) The New Right's repudiation of New Deal and Great Society liberalism
(D) The Federal Reserve's decision to nationalize major banks
items.stem: 'Reaganomics' rested on supply-side theory: lower taxes would unleash growth that paid for itself. Growth did return in the 1980s, but so did huge deficits and stark inequality. Which broader development best explains the context of this economic program?

stimulus.text: Reaganomics: tax cuts (1981), deregulation, and domestic spending cuts built on supply-side theory — with growth returning alongside large deficits and rising inequality.

items.explanation: The federal response — TARP bank bailouts — saved the financial system but was politically toxic: it fed populist fury on both left and right and deepened the institutional distrust that defines the period. The crisis context is deregulation plus the housing bubble; the political context is the backlash the rescue produced.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — the housing bubble's collapse in 2008 produced the worst financial crisis since the Depression; the government's bank bailouts (TARP) saved the system and fed a populist fury on both left and right

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the government intervened massively through TARP and other measures.
option_explanations.B: Right because the bailouts' political fallout — populist anger on both sides — shaped the decade that followed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the bailouts were deeply controversial, not consensual.
option_explanations.D: Wrong because the response added regulation (Dodd-Frank); it did not repeal all banking rules.

options: (A) The government's complete refusal to intervene in the financial system in any way
(B) TARP bailouts saved the banks but fed populist fury and distrust of institutions
(C) A unanimous national consensus that the bank bailouts were fair and necessary
(D) The immediate repeal of all federal banking regulation
items.stem: The 2008 financial crisis — the worst downturn since the Depression — was triggered by the collapse of a housing bubble built on deregulation and financial engineering. Which broader development best explains the political context of the federal response?

stimulus.text: The Great Recession (2007-2009): the housing collapse produced the deepest downturn since the Depression; TARP bank bailouts saved the system amid populist fury.

items.explanation: The claim matches the review's own framing: the ACA was the largest welfare-state expansion since the Great Society, it extended coverage to millions, and it became the decade's defining political war — fueling the Tea Party revolt. Each part of the claim is verifiable in the period's record.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — his Affordable Care Act (2010) extended health coverage to millions and became the decade's defining political war, fueling the Tea Party revolt; §Key terms (Affordable Care Act — the largest welfare-state expansion since the Great Society)

option_explanations.A: Wrong because the ACA was a domestic health-care law, not a foreign policy measure.
option_explanations.B: Wrong because the Great Society of the 1960s was itself a major welfare-state expansion.
option_explanations.C: Wrong because the law extended coverage to millions of previously uninsured Americans.
option_explanations.D: Right because the claim accurately places the ACA in the welfare-state lineage and its political fallout.

options: (A) The claim is wrong: the ACA only affected foreign policy
(B) The claim is wrong: no welfare-state expansion has occurred in America since the 1930s
(C) The claim is wrong: the ACA reduced the number of insured Americans nationwide
(D) The claim is reasonable — the largest welfare-state expansion since the Great Society
items.stem: The Affordable Care Act (2010) extended health coverage to millions. A student claims it was 'the largest expansion of the American welfare state since the 1960s.' Which of the following best evaluates this claim?

stimulus.text: The Affordable Care Act (2010): Obama's health-care law expanding insurance coverage to millions of Americans.
